label: The Staff
desc: Higher or lower. Nothing is named yet.
tip: The page is a picture of pitch: up there means up in sound. Read the second note against the first — that is all reading ever is.

cards.title: Five lines, and height is pitch
cards.body: The staff is a picture of pitch: higher on the page means higher in sound. That is the whole of it, and it is the only thing this study asks you to see.

cards.title: Read the second note against the first
cards.body: No names yet. Look only at where the second note sits compared to the one before it. Reading has never been anything else.

label: Steps and Skips
desc: Line to space is a step. Line to line is a skip.
tip: Do not count the notes between — see the shape. Neighbours are a step; anything that jumps a place is a skip. This is the eye you will read melodies with.

cards.title: Line to space is a step
cards.body: Next-door neighbours. The two notes touch: one on a line, the next in the space just above or below it.

cards.title: Line to line is a skip
cards.body: A place has been jumped. Line to line, or space to space — the eye catches the gap before you can count it.

cards.title: See the shape; do not count
cards.body: Counting the notes in between is what slow readers do. Steps and skips are two different pictures, and you will come to tell them apart at a glance.

label: The Landmarks
desc: Three notes learned by sight. Everything else is measured from them.
tip: Nobody reads by counting up from the bottom line. You learn a few anchors cold and read the rest as a distance from them. Three is enough to start.

cards.title: Three notes, learned cold
cards.body: Nobody reads by counting up from the bottom line. You memorise a few anchors and read everything else against them. These three are enough to start.

cards.title: Everything else is a distance
cards.body: One place above an anchor is a step above it; two places is a skip. That is how a reader reaches a note they never memorised.

label: First Position: Top Strings
desc: Read it, then play it. The letter is enough here — any octave.
tip: From now on the microphone answers for you. Do not hunt for the fret: read the note, hear it in your head, then let the hand go there.

cards.title: Now the microphone answers
cards.body: Read the note, hear it in your head, then let the hand go there. Do not hunt for the fret — hunting is the habit you are here to lose.

cards.title: Written an octave above what it sounds
cards.body: Guitar and bass are both notated an octave higher than they sound. It is universal, and it changes nothing for you: play the note you see.

cards.title: Any octave will do — for now
cards.body: This study passes on the letter alone. From the next one on, the octave counts as well.

label: First Position: Middle Strings
desc: The same, in the middle of the staff — and now the octave counts.
tip: One written note has five homes on the neck. In first position it has one, and that is the point: from here the reading and the hand are the same act.

cards.title: Now the octave counts too
cards.body: One written note has five homes on the neck. In first position it has one, and that is the point: from here, reading and the hand are a single act.

cards.title: The middle of the staff, the middle of the hand
cards.body: These notes sit on the lines you will look at most. Learn them here and the rest of the staff is measured outward from them.

label: Below the Staff
desc: The low strings, on their ledger lines.
tip: A ledger line is just the staff continuing where the page stopped drawing it. Count them outward in lines, never in notes.

cards.title: A ledger line is the staff, continued
cards.body: The page stopped drawing lines; the staff did not stop. A ledger line is one more line of the same ruler, drawn only where a note needs it.

cards.title: Count outward in lines, never in notes
cards.body: One ledger below, two ledgers below. Naming every note on the way down is exactly how a reader gets slow.

label: The Whole of First Position
desc: Every natural note under the hand, top to bottom.
tip: No string is announced any more. The note tells you where to go — that is the whole skill, and this is where it becomes one movement.

cards.title: No string is announced any more
cards.body: The note itself tells you where to go. That is the whole skill, and this is where it becomes one movement instead of two.

label: Accidentals
desc: Sharp, flat, natural — one semitone, written beside the note.
tip: A sharp raises by a semitone, a flat lowers by one, a natural cancels. On the neck that is exactly one fret in either direction — no more than that.

cards.title: Sharp, flat, natural
cards.body: A sharp raises the note by a semitone, a flat lowers it by one, a natural cancels either. Same place on the staff — a different sign in front of it.

cards.title: One semitone is one fret
cards.body: On the neck there is nothing to work out: a sharp is one fret higher, a flat one fret lower. The sign is the finger.

cards.title: It lasts until the barline
cards.body: An accidental holds for the rest of its bar, on that note, in that octave. At the next barline it is gone.

label: Key Signatures
desc: The signs stated once at the head, binding every bar that follows.
tip: The signature is not decoration: an F with a sharp at the head is an F sharp all the way down the page, in every octave, with nothing written beside it. Read the head first, always.

cards.title: Stated once, at the head
cards.body: Rather than a sign beside every note, the signs are gathered at the start of the line. Read the head first — always, before the first note.

cards.title: It binds every octave, all the way down
cards.body: An F with a sharp at the head is an F sharp everywhere on the page, in every octave, with nothing written beside it.

cards.title: A signature is a key
cards.body: One sharp is G major, two is D, one flat is F. In time you will recognise the key before you have read a single note.

label: Sight-Reading
desc: A line you have never seen, played straight through to a click.
tip: You will get one wrong. Keep going anyway — stopping to fix a note is the one habit that makes a reader unemployable. Eyes ahead of the hands.

cards.title: A line you have never seen
cards.body: Four bars, a click, one pass. Look at the shape before the first beat: where does it move by step, and where does it leap?

cards.title: The pitch, in its beat
cards.body: What is graded here is whether the right note was sounding while it was due. The millisecond belongs to the rhythm studies; this one is about not stopping.

cards.title: Keep going — especially when you are wrong
cards.body: You will miss one. Stopping to fix it is the single habit that makes a reader unusable. Eyes ahead of the hands.
